ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Pulmonology Consultation — Elizabeth Barrett Browning — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Pulmonology consultation with CT of the chest and spirometry, diagnosis of bronchiectasis, and the start of airway clearance

text.paragraph: Chronic productive cough for several years with occasional streaks of blood in the sputum and breathlessness on stairs, in a thin 39-year-old poet who had a chest illness with blood in the sputum about eight years ago and has taken prescribed oral morphine for many years. Please help exclude tuberculosis and nontuberculous mycobacterial disease, establish the diagnosis (bronchiectasis is suspected), plan its care, and advise on morphine and her lungs. [S]

Urgency: Urgent, within one week; she is stable, with streaks of blood only, and has been told to call 911 or go to the emergency department for more than a few teaspoons of blood, blood with breathlessness, or chest pain. She is masking in shared spaces until the smears are back. [S]

list.item: Can tuberculosis be excluded, and when can she stop masking?
What is the cause of her cough and blood-streaked sputum: bronchiectasis, nontuberculous mycobacterial disease, or another lesion such as a congenital malformation or a tumour?
If this is bronchiectasis, what work-up for its cause and what treatment do you advise, including airway clearance and an exacerbation plan?
How does long-term morphine affect her lung disease, and does the pulmonary view favour any change in the dose?
When should blood in the sputum send her to the emergency department, and does she need bronchial artery treatment now?

text.paragraph: Ms. Barrett Browning, a 39-year-old poet, is seen at the request of Dr. Haverford-Asante one week after her first visit. She describes a daily cough with three to four tablespoons of yellow sputum for several years, worse each winter, with about two chest infections a year that settle slowly, and streaks of blood every few weeks, never more than a thread; the last was three days ago. She becomes breathless on a flight of stairs. About eight years ago she coughed up blood during an illness that left her largely housebound since. She had a serious illness at about fifteen. She has never smoked and has no known exposure to tuberculosis. She has no sinus symptoms, heartburn, or joint problems. She takes morphine solution 10 mg twice daily, prescribed for years for cough, sleeplessness and palpitations; she has wondered whether it is bad for her chest. She would like to be able to go out in good weather and to keep writing. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Elizabeth Barrett was born on 6 March 1806 at Coxhoe Hall, about five miles south of Durham, the eldest child of Edward and Mary Moulton Barrett, and the eldest of twelve children; her father had added the surname Barrett as heir to his maternal grandfather's Jamaican estates. [D]

In 1821, while the family lived at Hope End in Herefordshire, she was seriously ill and went to the spa at Gloucester for treatment in June, returning to Hope End in May 1822; she later wrote, 'At fifteen I nearly died.' [D]

Her first editor reported that at about fifteen she injured her spine, by one account in a fall while saddling her pony, and by her son's statement through a strain while tightening the pony's girths, the injury not being discovered for some time; the editor judged that it contributed to the general weakness of health to which she was always subject. [D]
After the illness of 1821 she took opium by medical prescription, developing a lifelong habit. [D]

In 1838, after the family settled at 50 Wimpole Street, her health was in a very serious condition owing to the breaking of a blood-vessel; from then until her marriage she lived the life of an invalid. [D]
In August 1838 she moved to Torquay for her health, where her favourite brother Edward ('Bro') was her chief companion. [D]

On 11 July 1840 her brother Edward and two friends went sailing and did not return; the bodies were found three days later after a boat foundered in Babbacombe Bay. Her first editor wrote that she had the misery of thinking it was to attend on her that he had come to Torquay, that the place became a memory from which she shrank, and that even the sound of the sea became a horror to her. [D]

Her health suffered after the drowning; in the autumn of 1840 Mary Russell Mitford did not dare expect more than a few months of life for her, but she slowly gathered strength through the winter and returned to London in September 1841. [D]
Her brother Sam died in Jamaica in February 1840. [D]
Her mother died on 1 October 1828 after a last illness. [D]

On 2 October 1841 she wrote to H. S. Boyd that her case was 'not tubercular consumption, not what is called a decline, but an affection of the lungs which leans towards it', that a blood-vessel had broken three years before, and that four physicians, two experienced in diseases of the chest, agreed in that opinion. [D]
Her correspondence with the poet Robert Browning began in January 1845. [D]

list.item: Bronchiectasis, left lower lobe and lingula (J47.9). The CT confirms cylindrical bronchiectasis confined to the left lower lobe and lingula, which explains the daily sputum, the crackles, the mild obstruction and the streaks of blood from inflamed bronchial walls. The pattern and her history point to damage from a severe infection years ago. Normal immunoglobulins and a negative Aspergillus IgE exclude antibody deficiency and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis; nothing in her history suggests cystic fibrosis, a ciliary disorder or connective tissue disease, so those tests are not needed now. Haemophilus influenzae is the usual organism. Bronchiectasis Severity Index 3: mild. [S]

Tuberculosis, nontuberculous mycobacteria, and other lesions (J47.9). Three negative smears, a negative NAAT and a negative IGRA make tuberculosis very unlikely, and she no longer needs to mask; the cultures will be final in six to eight weeks. Nontuberculous mycobacteria, which favour thin women with bronchiectasis, cannot be excluded until the cultures are final; the tree-in-bud change is more likely from retained mucus, and the diagnosis would need two positive sputum cultures with compatible imaging. The CT shows no sequestration, mass or other lesion, so bronchoscopy is not needed. [S]

Morphine and the lungs (Z79.891). At 20 mg a day she shows no sedation or slowed breathing and her oxygen saturation is normal, so the dose is not dangerous to her lungs in itself. But morphine suppresses cough, and in bronchiectasis the cough is how she clears sputum; once airway clearance is established, a slow reduction would be reasonable if she wishes it. There is no pulmonary reason to change the dose urgently, and it should never be stopped abruptly. Codeine and other cough suppressants should be avoided, and naloxone kept at home. [S]
Blood in the sputum. Streaking only, from bronchiectasis, with no lesion needing treatment. Bronchial artery embolization is for large or repeated bleeding and is not needed. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Haverford-Asante's intake note and results. Three sputum samples: acid-fast smears negative and nucleic acid amplification negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis; mycobacterial cultures pending; routine culture Haemophilus influenzae, beta-lactamase negative. Interferon-gamma release assay negative; HIV test negative. Blood count normal with eosinophils 0.21 x10^3/uL; CRP 8.4 mg/L. Today: CT of the chest with contrast and thin-section reconstructions shows cylindrical bronchiectasis of the left lower lobe and lingula with bronchial wall thickening and mucus plugging, some tree-in-bud change in the left lower lobe, and no cavity, nodule, mass, lymph node enlargement or anomalous systemic artery; the upper lobes are clear. Spirometry after bronchodilator: FEV1 2.02 L (74% predicted), FVC 2.93 L, FEV1/FVC 0.69, with no significant bronchodilator response. IgG 1180, IgA 236 and IgM 142 mg/dL; total IgE 38 IU/mL; Aspergillus-specific IgE 0.08 kU/L. [S]

list.item: Stop masking: tuberculosis is very unlikely; follow the mycobacterial cultures to their final result at six to eight weeks, and repeat a mycobacterial culture yearly or with any unexplained decline. [S]

Airway clearance twice daily with the active cycle of breathing technique and an oscillating positive expiratory pressure device, taught by the respiratory physiotherapist this week, more often during exacerbations. [S]
A home exercise program to build strength and stamina, with weight-bearing exercise. [S]
Influenza vaccine yearly and a pneumococcal vaccine, with COVID-19 vaccination as recommended. [S]

A written exacerbation plan: for three days or more of worse cough, more or darker sputum and more breathlessness, send a sputum sample and start amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 14 days (chosen by her Haemophilus influenzae culture), and call the clinic. [S]
No long-term macrolide or inhaled antibiotic while she has fewer than three exacerbations a year; no inhaled corticosteroid without asthma. [S]
Sputum culture at each review and with every exacerbation; spirometry, Bronchiectasis Severity Index and a mycobacterial culture yearly. [S]

Morphine: no change for pulmonary reasons now; a slow reduction of about 10 percent at a time is reasonable if she chooses it once airway clearance is established; no codeine or other cough suppressants; naloxone at home. [S]
Call 911 or go to the emergency department for more than a few teaspoons of blood, blood with breathlessness, chest pain or dizziness; no bronchial artery treatment is needed now. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Haverford-Asante the same day, who continues the opioid review and the grief care. The CT was shown to Ms. Barrett Browning, who asked whether she had consumption and was relieved by the answer; she asked whether she could go out in good weather, and was told that fresh air and exercise will help her lungs. [S]

Follow-up: Pulmonology review if the mycobacterial cultures are positive, exacerbations reach three a year, blood returns in more than streaks, or the FEV1 falls; otherwise Dr. Haverford-Asante will follow the yearly checks. [S]
